analysis.one_liner: Sets nationwide patient-protection standards for HMOs and health insurers, including emergency care access and appeals rights.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote: after two hearings, it sat in the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee until the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required health insurers and HMOs to cover emergency care without prior approval, let patients choose their own doctors and see specialists directly, ban contract clauses that stop doctors from telling patients about treatment options or financial incentives, give patients a fast appeals process when care is denied, and force insurers to disclose how they pay doctors and where premium dollars go. It also opened the door for patients in employer plans to sue for injury or wrongful death under state law. It died in the Senate committee that held hearings on it, and no version of these protections became law in that Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Enrolled patients and their families — especially people with chronic conditions needing specialists, people needing emergency care, and anyone denied coverage — plus doctors, who would gain appeal rights and protection from gag clauses in insurer contracts.

how_it_helps.text: Requires insurers to cover emergency and urgent care around the clock without prior authorization whenever a prudent layperson would think it an emergency, including at hospitals outside the network [S2][S3].

Lets every enrollee pick a personal doctor from the network, guarantees direct access to specialists for chronic or special needs, and requires plans to offer a point-of-service option covering non-network providers at fair premiums [S2][S3].
Nullifies contract clauses that gag doctors from discussing their patient's health status, treatment options, utilization review rules, or the financial incentives that might affect their care [S3].

Creates a due-process system: utilization review criteria disclosed, reviewers paid regardless of denials, urgent-care authorization decisions within 30 minutes, appeals heard by independent same-specialty clinicians within 24 hours [S2][S3].

Bars insurers from discriminating against enrollees by health status, disability, age, race, gender, or income, and requires detailed public disclosure of what share of premiums goes to care versus administration, how reviewers overrule doctors, and what incentives might limit care [S2][S3].

Amends ERISA so state lawsuits for personal injury or wrongful death against companies administering employer health plans are no longer blocked by federal preemption, restoring a path to damages for injured patients [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and HMOs, which would face new coverage mandates, disclosure rules, appeals infrastructure, and liability exposure; costs would partly flow to premiums paid by employers and workers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employer health plans

drawbacks.text: New mandates — 24/7 emergency coverage, point-of-service options, disclosure and appeals infrastructure — would raise plan costs, and those costs would show up in premiums paid by employers and workers [S3].

Opening employer health plans to state personal-injury and wrongful-damage suits would raise insurers' and plans' liability exposure, an argument opponents used against all patients'-rights bills [S3].

The bill deliberately does not force plans to contract with every willing provider, so insurers would still control network size — protections for patient access stop at the network the insurer builds [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections target widely documented managed-care practices of the era — emergency-care denials, gag clauses, gatekeeping that blocked specialist access — and give patients real appeals and disclosure rights. The honest cost is higher premiums and more litigation risk, which insurers and employers argued would push some employers to drop coverage; the bill leaves insurers' core cost-control role intact, so the tradeoff favors patients but does not fundamentally restructure coverage.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, which held hearings on it twice, but the committee never voted to report it, and the bill died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Alfonse D'Amato introduced the bill on April 24, 1997, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources [S1][S5].
Five senators — three Democrats and two Republicans — cosponsored the bill [S4].
The committee held hearings on May 20, 1997, and again on March 24, 1998, but took no markup or vote on the bill [S5].
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, with the bill still in committee; Congress passed no comprehensive patient-protection law in that Congress [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and HMOs avoided the coverage mandates, disclosure rules, and expanded state-liability exposure, and employers sponsoring self-insured plans avoided the cost increases; patients kept the pre-1997 status quo, including the ERISA shield against damage suits.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll-call record; sponsorship was bipartisan, with a Republican lead sponsor and five cosponsors split three Democrats and two Republicans [S4].

industries.note: The bill would force insurers to cover emergency care without pre-approval, pay for out-of-network urgent and emergency services, open fast appeals, disclose how they pay and deny care, and face state damage suits. Insurers' cost-control and denial practices would be directly constrained, and premiums would rise.

Doctors would get direct specialist referrals for their patients, protection from contract gag clauses, due process before network termination, and an end to 'without cause' termination. Their clinical judgment would carry more weight against plan management.

ERISA plans would have to comply with the patient-protection standards and could face state personal-injury and wrongful-death suits, raising benefit costs. Employees in those plans would gain the same protections as individual-market enrollees.
